# Distributed tug fields {#sec-tug-fields}

The four-lane balanced cell has a second use beyond canceling steady momentum. If the lanes of a cell are sped up or slowed down along a stretch of ring, the structure feels a force along its length, and counter-propagating lanes contribute to that force with the same sign. This chapter derives that result, which is the paper's second primitive, and then asks what such a force does to the ring.

The right mental picture is not a rigid pipe with a single giant control thruster attached to it. It is a huge, lightly built but prestressed torus with many nearly axial lanes distributed around its wall, and selected neighborhoods of stator modules quietly speeding up or slowing down particular lanes over long distances.

What those neighborhoods can and cannot do follows from @sec-effective-tension. A tug is a force along the ring, and the ring answers it along the ring: as tension in the structure, as a shift of stream weight, and, when opposed sectors work against each other, as a sideways shift of the line along which the streams push. That makes the tug field the natural actuator for loads that act along the ring. It is a costly way to push the ring sideways, and @sec-tug-power-cost says how costly. Holding the ring's shape is left to @sec-collective-stability.

## Stationary spatial speed gradients act on momentum flux {#sec-stationary-spatial-speed-gradients}

The quantity being controlled is momentum flux along the ring centerline direction $s$.

Physically, one should imagine a control sector as a long run of stator hardware that does not grab the whole torus at once. Instead, it gently biases the speed of selected lanes over some distance, rather like a very long electromagnetic grade in a maglev line. The force on the structure comes from those distributed speed ramps.

Let one lane in a balanced cell have signed centerline speed

$$
V_s(s) = \pm u(s)
$$

with the upper sign for $+s$ travel and the lower sign for $-s$ travel. Here $u=v\cos\alpha$ is the scalar ring-centerline speed component.

For a stationary speed field, the convective acceleration along $s$ is

$$
a_s = V_s \frac{dV_s}{ds} = u \frac{du}{ds}.
$$ {#eq-convective-acceleration-s}

The key point is that $a_s$ is independent of the travel direction. A fixed spatial speed gradient acts the same way on counter-propagating lanes when projected onto the stationary structure.

For one lane with scalar mass flux $\dot m$, the structural force per unit ring length is therefore

$$
q_{s,\mathrm{lane}} = -\dot m \frac{du}{ds}.
$$ {#eq-tug-law}

If $\alpha$ is locally constant so that $u=v\cos\alpha$, this may also be written as

$$
q_{s,\mathrm{lane}} = -\dot m \cos\alpha \frac{dv}{ds}.
$$

That is the basic tug-field law.

## Why counter-propagating lanes add instead of canceling {#sec-counter-propagating-lanes-add}

Now consider a mirrored pair in the same fixed spatial speed gradient. If $du/ds>0$, the $+s$-traveling lane accelerates through the section while the counter-propagating lane decelerates through the same section. Yet their structural force densities are the same, because both are governed by the same stationary gradient law, @eq-tug-law.

So for one mirrored pair,

$$
q_{s,\mathrm{pair}} = -2\dot m \frac{du}{ds}.
$$ {#eq-tug-pair}

This is the real reason the pair adds instead of cancels. It is not that both lanes slow down in their own direction of travel. It is that a fixed spatial speed gradient produces the same structural reaction for both travel directions.

In more visual terms, a mirrored lane pair passing through one control sector behaves less like two carts hitting two brakes and more like two opposite traffic lanes passing through the same hill in the road. One stream is climbing while the other is descending, but the roadbed still feels the same net push in the same place.

Integrating across a control section from $u_1$ to $u_2$ gives

$$
F_{\mathrm{pair}} = -2\dot m (u_2-u_1).
$$ {#eq-tug-pair-integrated}

For $N_s$ participating paired modules in one azimuthal sector,

$$
F_{\mathrm{sector}} = -2N_s\dot m (u_2-u_1).
$$ {#eq-tug-sector}

If one only needs the magnitude, this becomes

$$
|F_{\mathrm{sector}}| = 2N_s\dot m |\Delta u|.
$$

For constant $\alpha$, $|\Delta u| = \cos\alpha |\Delta v|$.

## Distributed tug fields {#sec-distributed-tug-fields}

The control section need not be a hard boundary. In fact, a distributed transition is usually better because it lowers peak local force density.

That means the actuator is best imagined not as a point force but as a long, quiet patch of guideway that slightly changes lane speed over hundreds of metres or kilometres. The tug is smeared out along the structure instead of being applied at one violent station.

For one mirrored pair,

$$
q_{s,\mathrm{pair}}(s) = -2\dot m \frac{du}{ds}.
$$

For $N_s$ participating paired modules,

$$
q_{s,\mathrm{sector}}(s) = -2N_s\dot m \frac{du}{ds}.
$$

Integrating over the transition width gives

$$
F_{\mathrm{sector}} = \int q_{s,\mathrm{sector}}(s) ds = -2N_s\dot m \Delta u.
$$

So a distributed tug field preserves the same integrated authority as a hard transition while spreading the load over a useful finite distance.

## What a tug field does to the ring {#sec-tug-effects}

@sec-effective-tension gives the rules for reading the effect of any speed field. Effective tension is the same all round a free ring. The shape is the funicular of the load. Stream weight follows $1/u$. A tug field therefore does three different things, depending on how it is arranged round the tube and along the ring.

### All lanes together: tension in the structure {#sec-tug-hoop}

If every lane along a stretch of ring is sped up by the same fraction $\epsilon$, the momentum flux there rises by $\epsilon\Pi$, and the tugs at the two ends of the stretch pull it apart. By @eq-tug-reaction the structure's tension rises by the same $\epsilon\Pi$. The harder outward push of the faster streams is canceled by the inward pull of the tighter structure, and the ring's normal balance is unchanged.

So the first thing a tug field controls is how axial load is shared between streams and structure, station by station. That has uses. A membrane has to be kept taut. A structure 43,000 km long changes length by kilometres with temperature, and something has to take up the difference. And it is the channel through which loads applied along the ring are reacted (@sec-tug-purpose).

It is also a sizing rule. The structure must be able to carry $\epsilon\Pi$. In the reference case a speed modulation of one part in a thousand is 164 MN, which at a working stress of 1 GPa is 0.16 m² of material. At the density of a carbon composite, 1,600 kg/m³, that is about 260 kg/m out of a passive budget of 1,200 kg/m. Speed modulation of all lanes together is limited to parts in a thousand by structural mass before anything else limits it.

### All lanes together: stream weight {#sec-tug-weight}

At fixed mass flux, slugs bunch where they are slow, so a stretch of ring where the lanes run slow is heavier by @eq-weight-shift. This is the only way a speed field common to all lanes changes the ring's normal balance. It is weak: one part in a thousand of speed is 14 N/m, a little over a thousandth of the supported weight. And the ring answers it backward (@sec-funicular): the heavier stretch rises.

Weight trim is a slow, long-wave adjustment. Its proper use is to cancel a long-wave imbalance of load at its source, so that the ring's shape does not have to accommodate it.

### Opposed sectors: the thrust line {#sec-opposed-sectors-create-bending}

Now place tug fields of opposite sign in opposed azimuthal sectors of a torus of radius $a$. Then the sector tugs form a couple.

At the level of order of magnitude,

$$
M \sim 2a |F_{\mathrm{sector}}|.
$$ {#eq-couple}

A more explicit finite-sector estimate is

$$
M_{\mathrm{pair}} = 4aN_s\dot m |\Delta u| C_\mathrm{sec}(\Delta\phi)
$$ {#eq-couple-finite-sector}

with

$$
C_\mathrm{sec}(\Delta\phi) = \frac{\sin(\Delta\phi/2)}{\Delta\phi/2}
$$

where $\Delta\phi$ is sector width and $C_\mathrm{sec}$ accounts for finite angular extent.

@fig-opposed-cells sketches the opposed balanced four-cells geometrically: one cell runs from $A$ to $B$, while a mirrored cell runs from $A{\prime}$ to $B{\prime}$ on the opposite side of the guide shell. To keep the geometry readable, each plotted helix stands for the coincident positive and negative slug lanes of one handedness within that cell. @fig-opposed-cells-moment then makes the same logic more physical by resolving the lane reactions at representative control locations into local $s$- and $\theta$-components. The lane numbers from 1 to 8 are indicated in both @fig-opposed-cells and @fig-opposed-cells-moment for ease of bookkeeping.

![Two opposed balanced four-cells on a local guide-shell segment. One cell spans $A$ to $B$ and the other spans $A{\prime}$ to $B{\prime}$. Each helical path label 1-8 matches the lane numbers 1-8 used in @fig-opposed-cells-moment.](../figures/figure-5-opposed-balanced-cells-bending2.svg){#fig-opposed-cells}

![Local force-component view of the opposed balanced-cell actuator. Within each four-lane sum, the circumferential $F_\theta$ components cancel, while the ring-direction $F_s$ components add. In the opposed sectors, those surviving axial reactions push $A$ and $B$ apart while pulling $A{\prime}$ and $B{\prime}$ together, producing the bending couple sketched in @fig-opposed-cells.](../figures/figure-6-opposed-balanced-cells-moment.svg){#fig-opposed-cells-moment}

So the physical picture is two-stage. Within each balanced cell, the unwanted circumferential reaction is removed by symmetry. Across the torus, the surviving $s$-directed reactions push $A$ and $B$ apart while pulling $A{\prime}$ and $B{\prime}$ together, so the opposed sectors generate a couple rather than a mere net force.

What the couple does to the ring is best said in terms of the thrust line: the centroid of momentum flux over the tube's cross-section. With the streams faster on one side of the tube and slower on the other, the thrust line sits off the structure's own centroid by

$$
e = \frac{M}{\Pi} .
$$ {#eq-thrust-line-shift}

Treating the tube and its streams together as a beam with bending stiffness $EI$ and sideways load $q$, the balance of @eq-ring-equilibrium becomes

$$
EI\,y'''' + \Pi\,y'' = q - \left(\Pi e\right)'' .
$$ {#eq-beam-thrust}

The first term matters only for wavelengths shorter than $2\pi\sqrt{EI/\Pi}$, which is under 200 m for any plausible shell. Beyond that the streams, not the shell, decide the shape, and the solution with no load is simply

$$
y = -e .
$$ {#eq-structure-follows-thrust}

The structure moves sideways by the offset, in the opposite direction, and the thrust line stays where it was. The squeezed-hoop picture, in which opposed tugs bend the torus the way hands would, holds only below the 200 m crossover. At the wavelengths where the tug field was meant to act, the couple does not bend the ring. It slides the structure relative to the streams.

@fig-thrust-line shows this on a frame model: two chords 100 m apart, each carrying half the streams, joined by rungs and cross-bracing. With the bracing in place the structure's centerline takes up the mirror image of the commanded offset. With the bracing made a million times softer, so that there is no shear path between the chords, nothing moves, and each chord simply keeps its own tug as tension.

![A straight frame 20 km long carrying the reference streams in two chords 100 m apart. Opposed speed changes in the two chords offset the thrust line by up to 50 mm. With cross-bracing the structure moves by minus the offset. Without a shear path it does not move.](../figures/generated/thrust-line-shift.svg){#fig-thrust-line}

The offsets available are small. The illustrative 10 MN tug used later in this chapter, acting at the full 100 m arm, gives $M = 10^9$ N m and $e = 6$ mm.

### Load path from lane tug to thrust-line shift {#sec-load-path-lane-tug}

@eq-structure-follows-thrust is only available if the torus can carry the sector tugs across its cross-section as shear.

The intended free-body path is: lane force into lane carrier, lane carrier into rib or local cross-brace, rib into membrane hoop tension and circumferential shear, and then that distributed cross-sectional load closing against the opposed sector. In other words, the lane does not push directly on a rigid beam. It pushes on a ribbed shell that must redistribute the load around the torus cross-section.

A bookkeeping form that allows for an imperfect path is

$$
M_\mathrm{eff} \approx \eta_\mathrm{load} 2a |F_\mathrm{sector}|,
$$ {#eq-couple-effective}

where $\eta_\mathrm{load}$ is a cross-sectional transfer efficiency between zero and one that absorbs ovalization, shear lag, local twist, and other non-ideal shell behavior. The frame model gives the two limits: $\eta_\mathrm{load}$ is one when the wavelength is long compared with the shear-lag length $2\pi\sqrt{EI/GA}$, with $GA$ the shear stiffness of the cross-section, and it falls to zero when the wavelength is short compared with it. For a shell whose wall carries shear as readily as tension, that length is a few tube diameters.

The demand on the shell is modest. The shear force it has to carry is the slope of the couple, $V = d(\Pi e)/ds$. For the 10 MN example spread over a wavelength of 100 km that is about 60 kN on a cross-section 100 m across. If ribs or cross-braces are spaced every 10 m, the tug each sector hands to a bay is about 6 kN. That does not prove that $\eta_\mathrm{load}$ is near unity for a real membrane, but it does suggest that the shear path is not the hard part.

## Why fill and drain are not required for steady speed fields {#sec-fill-drain-required-steady}

The remaining concern is whether such speed modulation requires literal insertion and removal of slugs at every ordinary control section. For the architecture considered here, the answer is no.

Let slug number flux be $J$, so that

$$
\dot m = J m_s
$$

where $m_s$ is mass per slug. In steady flow through a lane with local speed $v(s)$, number continuity gives

$$
n(s) = \frac{J}{v(s)}
$$ {#eq-number-density}

where $n(s)$ is slug number density along the lane. Equivalently, if $h=1/J$ is time headway, then the center-to-center spacing in a locally uniform region is

$$
d(s) = \frac{1}{n(s)} = v(s)h.
$$

So a region with lower speed automatically compresses spacing and raises local occupancy, while a region with higher speed automatically expands spacing and lowers it. No source term is required. The lane stores more or less slug inventory simply because the same flux is moving more slowly or more quickly through that region.

That is the clean kinematic reason why ordinary tug fields do not require fill-and-drain hardware.

It is also important to state where the force actually comes from. The force is generated at the speed-gradient zones, not in a uniform low-speed pocket by itself. A closed low-speed pocket that returns to its starting speed has zero net integrated tug,

$$
\int -2\dot m \frac{du}{ds} ds = -2\dot m\Delta u = 0,
$$

so its entry and exit ramps produce equal and opposite tugs at different positions. Useful actuation therefore comes from placing those opposite gradient zones deliberately in space, so they put tension, a couple, or a transfer of load between streams and structure where it is wanted.

So the useful mental picture is not "the ring has a slow patch." It is "the ring has a deliberately placed slow-down ramp here and a deliberately placed speed-up ramp somewhere else," with the separation between those ramps creating the useful internal couple.

The main constraints are instead collision and delay limits. For a monotone low-speed region with minimum speed $v_1$, the minimum spacing becomes

$$
d_\mathrm{min} = h v_1
$$

so collision avoidance requires

$$
h v_1 \ge \ell_s + g_\mathrm{min}
$$ {#eq-collision-limit}

where $\ell_s$ is slug length and $g_\mathrm{min}$ is the minimum allowable gap.

For an upward ramp, incomplete actuation can let a trailing slug catch a slower incumbent. A useful first delay bound is

$$
\tau_d < \frac{h v_0 - (\ell_s + g_\mathrm{min})}{v_1-v_0}
$$ {#eq-delay-bound}

where $\tau_d$ is total sensing, computation, actuation, and field-establishment delay.

For time-varying control profiles, the continuity constraint is stronger still. The slug density must satisfy

$$
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (nV)}{\partial s} = 0.
$$ {#eq-continuity}

So the no-fill/no-drain claim applies only to steady or slowly varying speed fields. A controller cannot arbitrarily command $u(s,t)$ without launching density and headway waves through the lane. Dynamic control therefore requires phase and inventory management so that those waves do not create collision, starvation, or excessive headway error.

So the issue is not that mass must be added or removed in ordinary control sections. The issue is that the speed profile has to respect both static spacing limits and dynamic continuity.

## The tug actuator is also a high-power energy exchanger {#sec-tug-actuator-high-power}

The tug equations are momentum-flux equations, but the next question is about power, and rightly so.

For one lane, the exact finite power transfer across a section that changes speed from $u_1$ to $u_2$ is

$$
P_{\mathrm{lane}} = \frac{1}{2}\dot m\left(u_2^2-u_1^2\right) = \dot m \bar u \Delta u
$$ {#eq-lane-power}

where $\bar u=(u_1+u_2)/2$. For small $\Delta u$, this reduces to

$$
P_{\mathrm{lane}} \approx \dot m u   \Delta u.
$$

Using the force magnitude $|F_{\mathrm{lane}}| = \dot m |\Delta u|$, this is

$$
P_{\mathrm{lane}} \approx |F_{\mathrm{lane}}|\,u.
$$

At $u \sim 10~\mathrm{km/s}$, even modest structural tug implies enormous power exchange. A 1 MN tug at 10 km/s corresponds to roughly 10 GW handled: half of it taken out of the lanes that slow, half put into the lanes that speed up.

For a sense of scale on this ring, take a tug of 10 MN. That is the reaction of a 340-tonne vehicle accelerating along the ring at 3 g, or one part in sixteen thousand of the streams' momentum flux. At 10 km/s it implies about 100 GW of exchanged power.

If the notional 300-lane cross-section participates broadly, the mean integrated axial contribution is only about 33 kN per lane. The surprising quantity is therefore not force per lane. It is the power associated with making even a small speed change at 10 km/s.

That does not by itself kill the architecture, but it does mean the tug-field actuator is not a gentle trim system. It is a very high-power bidirectional momentum-and-energy exchanger. The paired-gradient argument gives local power balance only if the accelerating and decelerating channels are physically co-located, phase-matched, and tied together by a bidirectional electrical or magnetic power-transfer path. Otherwise the control sector is not a locally self-balancing actuator. It is a high-power grid node that must exchange power with a bus, buffer, or some other part of the ring.

Any serious realization would therefore require bidirectional power electronics, local energy buffering, phase-managed transfer between accelerating and decelerating lanes, and heat rejection for conversion losses.

Again, the helpful mental model is not a small trim tab. It is a distributed, reversible linear-motor system moving very large power between lanes and sectors while only modestly changing speed.

### Steering costs less than braking {#sec-tug-power-cost}

A tug works against the streams' forward motion, so every newton of tug handles $u$ watts. A sideways force on a slug does no work at all to first order. That asymmetry decides which actuator should do which job.

Take the thrust-line shift of @sec-opposed-sectors-create-bending and ask what it costs to hold a sideways load with it. A couple that varies sinusoidally along the ring with amplitude $M$ and wavenumber $k$ is equivalent, by @eq-beam-thrust, to a sideways load of amplitude $q_y = M k^2$. The tugs that make it have a density of $Mk/a$ over the two sectors, and so handle $Mku/a$ of power per unit length. The ratio is

$$
\frac{P'}{q_y} = \frac{u}{ak} = \frac{uL}{2\pi a}
$$ {#eq-tug-sideways-cost}

for a wavelength $L$. At 100 km that is 3.2 MW handled per metre of ring for every newton per metre of sideways load. Holding a load mismatch of 1% of the supported weight this way would keep 320 MW per metre circulating between counter-propagating lanes. At any realistic conversion efficiency that is not a control system. It is a heater.

Weight trim (@sec-tug-weight) is cheaper at the longest wavelengths but follows the same logic. A speed ripple $\epsilon$ shifts weight by $\lambda g_h\epsilon$ and handles $\Pi\epsilon k u$ of power per unit length, so

$$
\frac{P'}{q} = \frac{u^3 k}{g_h} .
$$ {#eq-weight-trim-cost}

That is 0.74 MW per metre for each newton per metre at a wavelength of 1000 km, and 34 kW per metre for two waves round the ring.

Set against these, recall from @sec-funicular what the ring does about a 1% mismatch at 100 km if nothing is commanded at all: its shape shifts by 0.15 m.

The conclusion is that tug fields are the wrong tool for holding the ring's shape. Sideways control should be done by sideways forces on the streams, which cost no power to first order. @sec-collective-stability shows how.

## Control-channel coupling and allocation {#sec-control-channel-coupling-allocation}

The tug channel is not dynamically independent. Spatial speed gradients generate structural tug, but the associated local speed field also changes helical prestress and stream weight.

This is the point where the machine stops looking like three separate knobs and starts looking like a coupled control surface. Turning the "tug" knob also nudges the local pressure and local weight because all three are functions of the same lane-speed field.

For the prestress channel,

$$
p_\mathrm{eq} \propto \dot m u \tan^2\alpha,
$$

so, at fixed $\dot m$ and $\alpha$, the first-order pressure sensitivity is simply

$$
\frac{\delta p_\mathrm{eq}}{p_\mathrm{eq}} = \frac{\delta u}{u}.
$$

For the normal balance, the streams taken alone push outward with

$$
q_\mathrm{lift} = 2N_p\dot m\left(\frac{u}{R} - \frac{g_h}{u}\right),
$$

whose sensitivity to speed is $2N_p\dot m\left(1/R + g_h/u^2\right)\delta u$. But the first of those two terms is the change in curvature force, and @eq-tug-reaction says the structure's tension cancels it exactly. What is left is the change in stream weight,

$$
\delta w = -2N_p\dot m\,\frac{g_h}{u^2}\,\delta u ,
$$ {#eq-weight-sensitivity}

which as a fraction of the supported load is

$$
\frac{\delta w}{w_p} = -\frac{g_h/u^2}{1/R - g_h/u^2}\,\frac{\delta u}{u}.
$$

At the illustrative 500 km, $u=10~\mathrm{km/s}$ reference point, that multiplier is about 1.4. So a 1% local speed increase lightens that stretch of ring by about 1.4% of the supported load.

The same speed field therefore actuates three coupled outputs: axial tug, local pressure, and local weight. A real machine would need a control-allocation layer that distributes commands across the four lanes and across neighboring sectors so that the three are separated as well as possible.

The right coupling metric is not just the local gradient. It is the speed-offset area associated with the tug command. Define

$$
\beta_w = \frac{g_h}{u^2}.
$$ {#eq-beta}

For the participating lane pairs in one control sector, the integrated weight side-effect is

$$
\Delta W_{\mathrm{sector}} = -2N_s\dot m\beta_w \int \delta u(s) ds.
$$

The associated tug from one gradient zone is still

$$
F_{\mathrm{sector}} = -2N_s\dot m \Delta u.
$$

So the coupling ratio becomes

$$
\frac{\Delta W_{\mathrm{sector}}}{F_{\mathrm{sector}}} = \beta_w \frac{\int \delta u(s) ds}{\Delta u}.
$$ {#eq-coupling-ratio}

If one defines an effective speed-offset length, called $L_\mathrm{eff}$, as the speed-offset area divided by the speed step, then a simple $\beta_w L$ estimate is just the special case in which that effective length happens to equal the physical sector length. A triangular ramp gives about $L_\mathrm{eff}=L/2$. A long low-speed pocket is dominated by its plateau length. An antisymmetric profile can partly cancel its own weight side-effect.

So the honest statement is this: the control coupling is governed by the speed-offset area associated with the tug command, not by the gradient alone.

At the illustrative 500 km, u = 10 km/s point, $\beta_w$ is about $8.4\times10^{-8}$ per metre, and the corresponding inverse length scale is about 11,800 km. Commands whose effective offset length is far shorter than that sit in a weak-coupling regime.

It is useful to separate three different smallness claims.

First, the required speed trim for a tug can be small because the moving mass flux is enormous. A 10 MN tug spread across 300 participating lanes is only about 33 kN per lane. With about $5.4\times10^{4}$ kg/s per lane, that implies a speed step of only about 0.61 m/s, or about $6\times10^{-5}$ of the 10 km/s operating speed.

Second, the weight side-effect per tug is small when the effective speed-offset length is short compared with 11,800 km. For a conservative 100 km box-like offset profile, the coupling factor is about 0.008, so a 10 MN tug carries about 84 kN of integrated weight side-effect. For a triangular profile of the same span, the side-effect is about half that.

Third, what that side-effect does to the ring is small. Spread over 1000 km it is under 0.1 N/m, less than a hundred-thousandth of the supported load, and by @eq-funicular it shifts the ring's shape by a few centimetres.

That is why the coupling can be ignored for most commands. The strong channel is axial tug. Pressure and weight are weak by-products unless the speed offset is held over thousands of kilometres, which is exactly what a deliberate weight trim does.

A useful way to name the allocation problem is with a local linearized control map. Write

$$
\delta y = \mathbf{S} \delta u
$$ {#eq-allocation-map}

with output vector

$$
\delta y = \left(\delta F_s,  \delta p_\mathrm{eq},  \delta w\right)^T
$$

and lane-command vector

$$
\delta u = \left(\delta u_1,  \delta u_2,  \delta u_3,  \delta u_4\right)^T.
$$

Here $\mathbf{S}$ depends on lane placement, handedness, sector participation, and operating point. The present paper does not solve that allocation problem, but naming it explicitly makes clear what the next control-theory step must be.

In plain language, the controller is trying to combine four lane-speed trims into three useful local effects, while suppressing the residual unwanted ones. That is a recognizable control-allocation problem, not handwaving.

## What tug fields are for {#sec-tug-purpose}

The ring is not creating net momentum from nowhere. A tugging sector must be paired with other sectors or stations that close the momentum and energy bookkeeping. What the architecture offers is a way to redistribute momentum flux, and the structural reaction that goes with it, along the ring. One sector borrows momentum and another pays it back, through smooth spatial speed fields in balanced four-lane cells, without monolithic moving hoops or routine fill-and-drain hardware.

With the effects and the costs laid out, the jobs that suit this actuator can be listed.

- **Loads along the ring.** A vehicle accelerating or braking on the ring, drag on a ring low enough to feel the atmosphere, and the horizontal pull of a leaning tether all act along the ring. By @eq-ring-equilibrium-parts such a load has to change the effective tension from one side of it to the other. A tug field at the point of application hands the load to the streams there, so the structure does not have to carry it round the ring as tension. This is the job the tug field does best, and here its power is not a cost. It is the point: the 100 GW that a 10 MN tug handles is the power being delivered to the vehicle.
- **Tension management.** Keeping the membrane taut, taking up thermal strain, and choosing where the structure carries load and where the streams do (@sec-tug-hoop).
- **Weight trim at the longest wavelengths.** Canceling slow, ring-scale imbalances of load at their source (@sec-tug-weight), within the cost of @eq-weight-trim-cost.
- **Small sideways trims at short wavelength.** Shifting the thrust line by millimetres (@sec-opposed-sectors-create-bending), where @eq-tug-sideways-cost is tolerable.
- **Spin-up, spin-down and momentum balance.** Bringing the streams to speed, and keeping the two travel directions balanced as loads come and go.

Holding the ring's shape is not on the list. That is a job for sideways forces on the streams, with one exception that @sec-ring-control arrives at: keeping the whole ring centered on the planet turns out to be weight trim at the longest wavelength there is.
